cases.learnTitle: Brain tumour on post-contrast T1, FLAIR and T2 (ReMIND-025)
cases.referenceSummary: Source manual tumour segmentation on the post-contrast T1 (ReMIND). Ventricle and cerebrum labels are automated source labels — shown for exploration only, never used for scoring. Images are defaced and dates are placeholders.
cases.learnNotes: Read each sequence for its job: FLAIR shows oedema and non-enhancing tumour bright with dark CSF; post-contrast T1 shows where the blood–brain barrier is disrupted; T2 shows CSF bright. Compare all three at the same level (two-up or four-up).

cases.learnTitle: Counting vertebral levels on CT (T1–L5 labels)
cases.clinicalContext: Radiotherapy planning CT of the torso.
cases.referenceSummary: Source segmentations of the whole vertebrae T1–L5 (body and posterior elements; semi-automatic, labelled level by level and verified by an expert). Lesions are not referenced in this pack, so the tasks are about level identification only.
cases.learnNotes: Count from a fixed landmark and say which you used: ribs articulate with T1–T12; the last rib-bearing vertebra is usually T12 and L1 is the first without ribs. The sagittal MPR shows the whole column at once; check your count on axial images.

cases.learnTitle: Mass on a left CC mammogram (CBIS-DDSM)
cases.referenceSummary: A digitised film mammogram (secondary capture, no pixel spacing — distances are not calibrated). The mass ROI comes from the CBIS-DDSM curation and is treated as an exploratory reference (self-review), not an authoritative key.
cases.learnNotes: Describe a mass by shape, margin and density relative to the surrounding tissue. One view is not enough to localise a mass in 3D; a real work-up needs the MLO view.

tasks.title: Find the abnormality on post-contrast T1
tasks.prompt: Scroll through the post-contrast T1 volume (MPR helps) and mark the centre of any abnormality, or state that there is none.

hints.text: Compare the two hemispheres at every level; look for asymmetry, mass effect or abnormal signal.
Jumping to a slice with the reference.
Reveal the reference answer.

tasks.explanation: A brain tumour is recognised by abnormal signal, mass effect (sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, midline shift) and, for many high-grade tumours, enhancement. The reference is the source's manual tumour segmentation.

tasks.title: Which series is FLAIR?
tasks.prompt: Compare the T2 and FLAIR series. On which one is CSF in the ventricles dark while oedema stays bright?

options.why: FLAIR nulls free water, so CSF is dark but oedema and most lesions remain bright.
On T2, CSF is bright — which can hide lesions next to ventricles and sulci.

hints.text: Look at the lateral ventricles on each series.

tasks.explanation: FLAIR is a T2-weighted inversion-recovery sequence that suppresses CSF signal, making periventricular and cortical oedema easier to see.

tasks.title: Describe the lesion across sequences
tasks.prompt: Describe the lesion: location (lobe, side), size, signal on FLAIR/T2, enhancement, and mass effect. Give a short differential.

hints.text: Use the four-up layout to see post-contrast T1, FLAIR and T2 at once.

tasks.explanation: The source provides a tumour segmentation, not a histology label for this view, so the description is self-reviewed against the checklist and the book's brain tumour section.

rubric.text: Lobe, side and intra- vs extra-axial location
Signal on FLAIR/T2 and the extent of surrounding oedema
Mass effect: sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, midline shift
Differential that fits the image features (e.g. primary glioma vs metastasis)

tasks.title: Oral exam: show it, describe it, defend it
tasks.prompt: As if presenting to an examiner: (1) show the key finding with an arrow, (2) describe it in one sentence (location, size, pattern), (3) give your leading interpretation with the image evidence for it, and (4) explain why a solitary metastasis or an abscess is less likely.

hints.text: Keep it to four sentences. Examiners reward a clear search pattern and an honest statement of what the images cannot tell you (MRI suggests but does not prove tumour type or grade).

tasks.explanation: There is no automatic grader for free-text reasoning. Compare your answer with the checklist and the linked book pages.

rubric.text: Showed the finding on the right series and slice
One-sentence description with location, size and pattern
Leading interpretation supported by named image features
Closest alternative (a solitary metastasis or an abscess) addressed with opposing evidence
Stated what needs comparison, other sequences/phases, or clinical information

tasks.title: Find the L1 vertebral body
tasks.prompt: Mark the L1 vertebral body. Use the sagittal MPR to count, and note which landmark you counted from.

hints.text: Open MPR (axial / coronal / sagittal) and work in the sagittal view.
Find the lowest vertebra with a rib attached; that is usually T12.
Showing the reference outline.
Reveal the reference answer.

tasks.explanation: Level errors are common; a mark in the neighbouring vertebra is reported as 'lies in the reference for T12/L2…' so you see by how many levels you were off. Transitional anatomy can change the count — always state your landmark.

tasks.title: Find and describe the mass
tasks.prompt: Search this mammogram, box any mass you find, and describe its shape, margin and density.

hints.text: Compare regions of glandular tissue; a mass has convex borders and is seen as a discrete density.
Reveal the reference answer.

tasks.explanation: Mass descriptors (shape, margin, density) carry most of the diagnostic weight in the book's approach. This ROI is a curated research annotation used here for comparison only; the image has no calibrated spacing, so tolerances are in pixels.

rubric.text: Noted that a second view is needed to localise it
